lesson.title: Numbered and Tracked: What a TCP Segment Adds to Your Data
lesson.summary: A TCP segment is a transport-layer unit consisting of a header and a chunk of an application's byte stream, and its sequence numbers are what let TCP detect loss and reassemble data correctly despite the packet-switched network beneath it.
lesson.body:
TCP treats the data an application sends, a file being uploaded, an email being composed, as one continuous, ordered stream of bytes rather than a series of separate messages. Since a single IP packet can only carry so much payload before it exceeds the network path's maximum transmission unit, TCP breaks that stream into pieces, and each piece, combined with a TCP header, is called a segment. A segment is the transport-layer unit specifically associated with TCP, and it is what actually rides inside an IP packet's payload on its journey across the network described in the previous chapter.

The TCP header, a standard 20 bytes and extendable to 60 with options, carries the fields that make reliable delivery possible. A 2-byte source port and 2-byte destination port identify which application on each end the data belongs to. A 4-byte sequence number and 4-byte acknowledgment number are the real workhorses: because TCP is moving one continuous byte stream, the sequence number tells the receiver exactly which byte offset within that stream this particular segment's payload starts at. That single piece of information is what lets segments that arrive out of order, which happens routinely given the packet-switched routing covered in the last chapter, be reassembled into the correct order at the receiving end, and it is also what lets the receiver notice precisely which bytes never arrived at all.

Working through a concrete case makes this click. Suppose you upload a 5,000 byte photo over a TCP connection, and the network path allows about 1,400 bytes of TCP payload per segment. TCP splits the photo into four segments carrying roughly 1,400, 1,400, 1,400, and 800 bytes, with sequence numbers marking byte offsets 0, 1400, 2800, and 4200. If the third segment, the one starting at offset 2800, is lost somewhere along the path, the receiver notices a gap: it has bytes up through 1400 to 2799, and separately it has bytes starting at offset 4200, but nothing covering offset 2800 through 4199. TCP can then trigger retransmission of specifically that missing range rather than resending the entire photo from scratch, which is exactly why the sequence number exists.

There is a terminology point worth being precise about, since it sets up the next chapter directly. RFC 9293, TCP's current specification, referenced earlier as the document that formally obsoletes the original RFC 793, uses the word segment specifically because TCP is connection-oriented and stream-based, tracking an ongoing, stateful conversation between two endpoints. TCP's sibling transport protocol, UDP, does not organize data this way at all and does not call its unit of data a segment. It calls it a datagram, and that difference in name reflects a genuinely different design philosophy, which the next chapter takes up directly.

Segments tie the layers covered so far into a single chain: a chunk of application data becomes a TCP segment, measured in the bytes from several chapters back, that segment typically travels inside exactly one IP packet, and that packet is carried inside a fresh frame at every physical hop between the sending device and the receiving one.
